doc.title: Arturo Sandoval interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 12, 2023

title: How he scores films and how he got the Clint Eastwood job
summary: He watches the film and improvises at the keyboard; the story of Andy Garcia's phone call and Eastwood hiring him for the whole score of The Mule and Richard Jewell.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: So what’s the first thing, the very first thing that you do to get started when you get a description of a project and maybe a — not a script but you know here’s the story, here’s what we want to happen.

Okay. I’m going to share with you a secret. When I do things for movies, by the way you know I don’t know if you are aware that I wrote the last two scores for Clint Eastwood. You know? I wrote “The Mule” and “Richard Jewell.” I wrote those two scores for him. They sent me — don’t repeat that — they always send me the script and I read the title. I said oh my goodness, I don’t have time to read a hundred pages of a script. No, no, no, no. Show me the movie, man. Show me the thing. And the way I compose or write the score, I put the movie there on. And then I sit down at my keyboard on the piano. I’m watching the things and I see when it’s a place or room where the music could intervene without obstructing the dialogue or making too much emphasis in the drama, which is, you know, another thing we have to be careful. Our mission is to enhance the whole thing, but without interfering. You see what I mean? It’s interesting process. It’s no good to get your — past the line in other words you understand what I mean? You have to contribute but don’t try to be a protagonist. You are a function of the drama. That’s your mission. I’m going to share with you a story, very funny story. I met Clint Eastwood two, three times over the years, in jazz clubs in town and different places you know, very briefly. About four or five years ago I was in the house of a very dear friend of mine. Maybe you are familiar with the name Mr. Frank Mancuso. He was the president of Paramount and MGM for many years. He’s a very dear friend. He smoked Fuente like me, and we were having a cigar in his backyard, and then my phone rings. I pick it up and that was Andy Garcia you know. Andy played me in the movie on HBO. Okay. We are very close. We are good friends. And he’s a very close friend of Mr. Mancuso as well. And then Andy is a guy of very few words. And he said, “Arturo, pay attention to your phone. Clint Eastwood is going to call you.” And he hung up. I says, “Oh my goodness.”

I talked to him on Friday and I said, “Hey, that was Andy. He said Clint Eastwood was going to call me. What is this?” Okay, the phone rang, I get, the thing is, “Arturo, how are you, this is Clint.” Okay. And then he said, “Arturo I’m doing a movie and there’s a scene there, it’s less than three minutes.” This is a very interesting story. He said, “There’s a scene there that I want you to write a cue, it’s less than three minutes, it’s a big party in the swimming pool of the guy” blah-blah. “And the people are dancing, Latino music, and I want you to do that for me.” “It would be my honor and my pleasure, sir.” And then okay we agreed to meet in his office to see the movie, and then I thought about it for a minute and then I brought my keyboard with my speakers and my sound engineer to help me to connect everything. I thought that Clint was going to show me that specific cue. But no, he played the movie from the top. And I got my keyboard there. Every time I see the opportunity I put my hands there and improvised things. He looked at me once in a while, he looked at all the producers on the set, and then he scratched his head and said, “Okay that was two hours.” “It was?” “Yeah. He played the whole movie for me. Nobody said a word but I was playing every time I saw the opportunity. When we get to the end he looked at me and he said, “Arturo, I just changed my mind, I want you to write the whole score.” I said, “Yes!”
